frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Belimo Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current HVAC actuators, valves, and sensors, sold to commercial building manufacturers and through controls contractors and system integrators.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Belimo.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home energy‑management system) sold directly to homeowners.
2) Expand the existing commercial product line into adjacent commercial segments (e.g., industrial HVAC) without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B commercial building manufacturers and system integrators.
4) License Belimo's technology to consumer brands for white‑label HVAC products, retaining control over design and branding.
5) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop a consumer‑focused HVAC product, sharing R&D and distribution costs.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo's residential HVAC products if they perceive the products as energy‑efficient and smart, because they value lower utility bills and environmental impact.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking cost‑of‑ownership savings and eco‑friendly solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of energy costs and ENERGY STAR certification creates a willingness to pay a premium for products that deliver measurable savings.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can charge a premium price for ENERGY STAR‑certified residential products and capture margin through higher unit prices and potential subscription services for smart home integration.
assumptions: Homeowners are price‑sensitive but willing to pay a premium for energy‑efficiency.
ENERGY STAR certification is a credible signal of performance.
Belimo can reach homeowners through existing OEM channels or direct sales.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show at least 40% indicating they would purchase a Belimo residential product if it was ENERGY STAR certified and priced 10% above a comparable non‑certified product.
Sales of ENERGY STAR‑certified residential products would increase in regions with higher energy costs.
Homeowners would be more likely to recommend a product that demonstrably reduces their utility bills.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo's residential HVAC products if they perceive the products as energy‑efficient and smart, because they value lower utility bills and environmental impact.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Belimo's residential products if they trust the brand for reliability and durability, because they want long‑term performance and minimal maintenance in their homes.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who prioritize durability and low‑maintenance systems.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A reputation for quality and reliability reduces perceived risk of product failure, leading buyers to choose Belimo over competitors.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo can command premium pricing for high‑quality residential products and capture value through repeat purchases and reduced warranty claims.
assumptions: Homeowners associate Belimo with superior product quality.
Reliability is a primary purchase driver for residential HVAC products.
Belimo's existing B2B reputation transfers to consumer perception.
predictions: A survey of homeowners would show at least 30% indicating they would choose a Belimo product over a competitor if it was marketed as reliable and durable.
Reliability would be a top reason for repeat purchases of Belimo residential products.
Homeowners would be less price‑sensitive when reliability is emphasized.

X1.name: Homeowner Preference Test for Belimo Residential Products
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners who have a central HVAC system, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents who would purchase a Belimo residential product at a given price point, and the average WTP (in euros) for each product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of respondents will choose the ENERGY STAR‑certified Belimo product at a price 10% above a comparable non‑certified product.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% of respondents will choose the Belimo product when reliability and durability are emphasized, and the average WTP will be higher than the ENERGY STAR‑certified product.

X1.decision_rule: If the ENERGY STAR‑certified product achieves at least 40% purchase intent and a WTP at least 10% above the non‑certified product, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on energy‑efficiency. If the reliability‑emphasized product achieves at least 30% purchase intent and a WTP at least 10% above the ENERGY STAR‑certified product, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on reliability. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Belimo already offers residential HVAC products and emphasizes energy efficiency, but no source demonstrates homeowner willingness to pay a premium for ENERGY STAR certification. A proposed survey test (X1) is needed to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity before committing to any consumer expansion.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with central HVAC systems who are price‑sensitive but value energy‑efficiency savings.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated residential product line that is ENERGY STAR‑certified and marketed as a cost‑of‑ownership‑saving solution, leveraging Belimo’s existing OEM and system‑integrator relationships.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 6‑week, €18,000 online survey test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for an ENERGY STAR‑certified residential product.
final.uncertainty: The size of the premium homeowners are willing to pay for energy efficiency and whether Belimo’s residential brand reputation translates to consumer trust.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent below 40% or willingness to pay significantly below a 10% premium over a comparable non‑certified product, the investment would be reconsidered.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a private, convenient, and affordable way to learn a life-saving skill, because they value flexibility and avoid public classes.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who want to prepare for cardiac emergencies without attending formal training.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently avoid public classes due to stigma, time constraints, and lack of privacy. A home kit removes these barriers, making CPR learning accessible and socially acceptable.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell premium-priced home kits directly to consumers, generate recurring revenue through optional add-ons (e.g., family training modules), and capture data for personalized learning.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for home CPR kits.
Privacy concerns are a significant barrier to public class attendance.
Consumers trust Laerdal's brand to deliver effective training.
predictions: A survey of potential consumers will show >50% would purchase a home CPR kit at a price of $30-$50.
Purchase intent will be higher for kits marketed as private and flexible compared to public classes.
Repeat purchase rate for optional family training modules will be above 20%.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a private, convenient, and affordable way to learn a life-saving skill, because they value flexibility and avoid public classes.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a family-friendly, educational tool that fosters shared learning and social responsibility, because they value community and intergenerational connection.
T2.who_benefits: Families and individuals who want to teach children and others about CPR while strengthening family bonds.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers are motivated by the desire to create a safe environment for their loved ones and to contribute to community health. A home kit that emphasizes family participation and shared learning reduces the stigma of public classes.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell premium-priced family kits with optional training sessions, generate recurring revenue through subscription-based family modules, and capture data for personalized family training.
assumptions: Families are willing to invest in home CPR training as a shared activity.
Social messaging about family safety and community health drives purchase.
Consumers trust Laerdal's brand to deliver effective family training.
predictions: A survey of potential families will show >40% would purchase a home CPR kit for family training at a price of $30-$50.
Purchase intent will be higher for kits marketed as family-friendly compared to kits marketed as individual training.
Repeat purchase rate for optional family training modules will be above 25%.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home devices.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training framed as a family safety precaution, supported by evidence of home cardiac arrest prevalence and Laerdal’s existing home CPR program. Conduct a low‑cost messaging test to validate consumer demand before full development.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a safety precaution for household members, because they perceive home cardiac arrest as a personal risk and are willing to pay for peace of mind.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for a cardiac emergency at home.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of home cardiac arrest prevalence and a desire to protect loved ones creates a personal motivation to learn CPR before an emergency occurs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal would sell premium-priced home CPR kits directly to consumers, capture recurring revenue through optional training modules or subscription services, and build a brand of personal safety.
assumptions: Consumers trust Laerdal's reputation in healthcare education to indicate safety.
Price sensitivity is low enough for consumers to accept premium pricing for home use.
Marketing can effectively communicate the personal safety benefit to homeowners.
predictions: A survey of homeowners will show higher intent to purchase a home CPR kit when framed as a family safety product versus a professional training kit.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with stated concern about home cardiac arrest.
Repeat purchase or subscription rates will be higher for home kits than for professional kits.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a safety precaution for household members, because they perceive home cardiac arrest as a personal risk and are willing to pay for peace of mind.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is integrated into existing home safety routines (e.g., smoke detectors, emergency kits) because they view preparedness as part of general home safety, leading to lower purchase friction.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who already purchase safety products and are comfortable with integrating new devices into their home environment.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A habit of purchasing safety devices makes home CPR training feel like an additional, familiar item, reducing perceived risk and effort.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal would sell home CPR kits as an add-on to existing safety products, leveraging existing consumer channels and capture recurring revenue through accessories or upgrades.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to purchase safety devices from trusted brands.
Home CPR training is perceived as a low-effort, low-risk addition to existing safety routines.
Retail distribution channels can reach homeowners effectively.
predictions: A survey of homeowners will show higher purchase intent for home CPR kits when presented as an add-on to safety products versus a standalone product.
Purchase intent will be positively correlated with stated frequency of purchasing safety devices.
Sales will be driven by cross-selling rather than premium pricing alone.

X1.name: Home CPR Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are homeowners (n=300) recruited via a panel. They view a product description of a home CPR kit and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Not interested" to 7 "Very interested"). The description is framed in two ways: (A) "Family safety precaution" (emphasizing protection of household members). (B) "Add-on to existing home safety routines" (emphasizing integration with smoke detectors, alarms, etc.).
X1.sample: 300 homeowners recruited from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each messaging condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will yield a mean score ≥ 5.5 and significantly higher than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will yield a mean score ≥ 5.5 and significantly higher than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If Condition A mean ≥ 5.5 and Condition B mean < 5.5, recommend developing a consumer proposition framed as a family safety precaution (support T1). If Condition B mean ≥ 5.5 and Condition A mean < 5.5, recommend developing a consumer proposition framed as an add-on to safety routines (support T2). If both means are below 5.5, recommend no expansion.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training framed as a family safety precaution, supported by evidence of home cardiac arrest prevalence and Laerdal’s existing home CPR program. Conduct a low‑cost messaging test to validate consumer demand before full development.
final.target_customer: Homeowners who are concerned about the safety of their household members and are willing to invest in preparedness.
final.value_proposition: A home CPR kit positioned as a personal safety precaution for family members, offering privacy, flexibility, and the ability to train multiple household members, with optional training modules and subscription services.

final.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent and willingness to pay for a home CPR kit are unknown. The test will determine whether consumers will adopt the product as a personal safety precaution versus an add‑on to existing safety routines.
would_change_if: If the messaging test shows Condition B mean ≥ 5.5 and Condition A mean < 5.5, the recommendation would shift to an add‑on‑to‑safety‑routines proposition.
If the test shows both conditions below 5.5, the recommendation would be to maintain the current focus on professional training and not expand into consumer markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home devices.

T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased public awareness of home cardiac arrests and the success of bystander CPR in public cases creates a perceived need for home preparedness.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell premium-priced home CPR kits directly to consumers, generate recurring revenue through optional training modules or subscription services, and build brand trust through family-focused messaging.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that can save lives.
Marketing can effectively communicate the safety and preparedness benefits to homeowners.
Distribution channels (e.g., online, retail) can reach target consumers.
predictions: A survey of homeowners will show higher intent to purchase a home CPR kit if framed as a family preparedness product.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Kit
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners (ages 25-55) recruited via a panel, stratified by home ownership and health-tracking device ownership.
X1.measure: 1) Intent to purchase a home CPR kit (binary: "Would you buy this kit?"). 2) WTP (EUR) for the kit. 3) Preference for messaging: "family preparedness" vs. "health wellness add-on" vs. "no purchase".

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the "family preparedness" messaging condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the "health wellness add-on" messaging condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the "family preparedness" condition achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% and WTP ≥ €30, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners. If the "health wellness add-on" condition achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% and WTP ≥ €30, develop a consumer proposition integrated with smart health devices. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not expand into consumer markets.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that positions it as a personal health responsibility, leveraging Laerdal's professional brand credibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a personal health responsibility and delivered through a trusted brand, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies and feel a personal responsibility to act.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR as a professional task to a personal duty when they see it framed as a health responsibility and when they trust the brand associated with professional medical expertise.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium pricing for consumer kits, subscription models for ongoing training, and direct-to-consumer sales that leverage its brand credibility.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to invest in personal health preparedness.
The brand association with Laerdal's professional medical reputation transfers to consumer perception.
A differentiated consumer proposition can be developed within budget and time constraints.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused CPR kit, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic health product.
Willingness to pay will be above the price point of a standard health product.
Customers will report higher perceived trust in the brand compared to competitors.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a personal health responsibility and delivered through a trusted brand, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is integrated into existing consumer health routines and recommended by trusted health professionals, leading to higher adoption rates and repeat purchases.
T2.who_benefits: Health-conscious consumers who already engage in daily health activities and trust professional medical recommendations.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers adopt new health products when they see them as part of a familiar routine and when they receive endorsement from trusted professionals, reducing perceived risk and increasing perceived benefit.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can capture value through bundled consumer health products, subscription services for routine check-ins, and partnerships with healthcare providers to recommend the kit.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to integrate new health products into their daily routines.
Health professionals' recommendations significantly influence consumer purchase decisions.
A differentiated consumer proposition can be positioned as a complement to existing health habits.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused CPR kit bundled with a daily health routine product, adoption rates will be higher than for a standalone CPR kit.
Consumers will report higher intent to purchase when the kit is recommended by a healthcare professional.
Repeat purchase rates will be higher for consumers who received a recommendation versus those who chose the product independently.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Personal Responsibility vs Professional Recommendation
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a consumer-focused CPR kit description (positioned as a personal health responsibility) or a professional recommendation version (positioned as endorsed by healthcare professionals). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 500 adults in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and health awareness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each exposure version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the personal responsibility version compared to the professional recommendation version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the professional recommendation version compared to the personal responsibility version.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the personal responsibility version is at least 10 points higher than for the professional recommendation version, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on personal responsibility. If the difference is less than 5 points, consider a hybrid model combining personal responsibility and professional endorsement. If the difference is less than 2 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time.

revisions.reason: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer purchase behavior, purchase intent, or willingness to pay for home CPR training. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that positions it as a personal health responsibility, leveraging Laerdal's professional brand credibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Individual consumers who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies and feel a personal responsibility to act, particularly those who already engage in daily health activities.
final.value_proposition: A consumer-focused CPR kit that is delivered through a trusted brand, offering flexible, private learning and the ability to share with family members, resulting in higher purchase intent and willingness to pay compared to generic health
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a personal responsibility versus professional recommendation exposure. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a full
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a consumer CPR kit and the extent to which professional endorsement influences purchase decisions are uncertain. The pilot will provide the necessary data to resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for the personal responsibility version is at least 10 points higher than for the professional recommendation version, we would proceed with a consumer proposition focused on personal responsibility.

If the pilot shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two exposure versions, we would reconsider the investment and explore alternative strategies such as a hybrid model or no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether Laerdal Medical should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current healthcare and training products, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach is unknown; must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, and ability to capture value.
Investment must be justified by clear value capture mechanisms (e.g., premium pricing, subscription, or direct-to-consumer sales).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals).
2) Expand existing B2B products into new B2B segments (e.g., larger training organizations, hospitals).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current healthcare and training products for professionals.
4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑brand or distribute existing products under a consumer brand.
5) License the core CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers for integration into home devices.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a private, convenient, and affordable way to learn a life-saving skill, because they value flexibility and avoid public classes.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers who want to learn CPR without attending formal classes.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently avoid public classes due to stigma, time constraints, and lack of privacy. A private, home-based solution removes these barriers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell kits directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through optional add-ons (e.g., advanced training modules), and build a subscription model for updates.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a private, home-based CPR kit.
The product is easy to use and provides sufficient practice for effective learning.
Marketing can effectively communicate the convenience and privacy benefits.
predictions: Consumers will purchase a home CPR kit at a price point above the $30 Mini Anne kit.
Purchase intent will be higher among adults who have not taken a formal CPR class.
Repeat purchase or subscription rates will be higher than for a one-time purchase.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a private, convenient, and affordable way to learn a life-saving skill, because they value flexibility and avoid public classes.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a family-friendly, educational tool that teaches a life-saving skill to children, because parents want to prepare their families for emergencies.
T2.who_benefits: Parents of children who want to teach them CPR and other emergency skills.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Parents are increasingly concerned about child safety and want to equip their families with skills that could save lives. A home-based program that involves children makes learning feel like a shared family activity.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal can sell kits to families at a premium price, offer subscription-based updates for new skills, and bundle with educational content to increase average transaction value.
assumptions: Parents are willing to invest in home training for their children.
The product can be marketed as a family activity rather than a professional training tool.
The content is age-appropriate and engaging for children.
predictions: Parents will purchase a home CPR kit for their children at a price point above the $30 Mini Anne kit.
Purchase intent will be higher among parents with children under 12.
Repeat purchase or subscription rates will be higher than for a one-time purchase.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a family-friendly, educational tool that teaches a life-saving skill to children, because parents want to prepare their families for emergencies.

If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend no expansion.

final.uncertainty: The actual demand for a DIY insulation kit is unknown; evidence shows homeowners are aware of insulation options but do not show purchase intent or willingness to pay a premium. Safety and compliance concerns remain uncertain.

Visitors are randomly assigned to either variant and tracked for conversion and repeat purchase.
X1.sample: 2,000 UK homeowners (1,000 per variant) recruited via an online panel, screened for intent to purchase insulation in the next 12 months.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kingspan Group plc investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B insulation and building envelope products.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY users for a specific use case (e.g., home insulation, small-scale building).
2) Expand the existing B2B insulation and building envelope products into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., broader distribution, new product lines).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B construction professional market.
4) Partner with or license the existing insulation technology to consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer brand.

X1.name: DIY vs Incentive Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from UK homeowners (n=200) and randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: DIY-focused (emphasizing ease, cost savings, and self-installation) or incentive-focused (emphasizing government/local retrofit scheme rebates and deep retrofit benefits). Both conditions include a product description of Kingspan's consumer insulation kit and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.
X1.sample: 200 UK homeowners (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, home ownership, and region.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average WTP (in euros) for the Kingspan insulation kit in each condition. Secondary measure: self-reported intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than incentive condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Incentive condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than DIY condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the DIY condition exceeds the average WTP in the incentive condition by at least €20 (or a 15% increase), proceed to develop a differentiated DIY consumer proposition. If the incentive condition exceeds DIY by at least €20, recommend expanding the existing B2B products into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition. If neither condition exceeds the other by the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on the current B2B market.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Kingspan already sells direct to end-users and offers DIY guidance, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners will purchase insulation as a DIY project. A limited test (DIY vs incentive messaging) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources.

final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Kingspan's insulation as an easy-to-install, cost-effective DIY solution, leveraging existing direct-to-consumer channels and guidance.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 DIY vs incentive messaging test with 200 UK homeowners to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual purchase intent, and the effectiveness of DIY framing versus incentive messaging are uncertain. Evidence of consumer demand is limited to company claims and does not prove real sales.
would_change_if: If the test shows the DIY condition generates at least €20 more average willingness to pay than the incentive condition, we would proceed to develop a differentiated DIY consumer proposition.

arguments.name: DIY vs Incentive Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from UK homeowners (n=200) and randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: DIY-focused (emphasizing ease, cost savings, and self-installation) or incentive-focused (emphasizing government/local retrofit scheme rebates and deep retrofit benefits). Both conditions include a product description of Kingspan's consumer insulation kit and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.
arguments.sample: 200 UK homeowners (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, home ownership, and region.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average WTP (in euros) for the Kingspan insulation kit in each condition. Secondary measure: self-reported intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).

prediction_by_theory.T1: DIY condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than incentive condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Incentive condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than DIY condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP in the DIY condition exceeds the average WTP in the incentive condition by at least €20 (or a 15% increase), proceed to develop a differentiated DIY consumer proposition. If the incentive condition exceeds DIY by at least €20, recommend expanding the existing B2B products into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition. If neither condition exceeds the other by the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on the current B2B market.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Kingspan already sells direct to end-users and offers DIY guidance, but it does not demonstrate that homeowners will purchase insulation as a DIY project. A limited test (DIY vs incentive messaging) is needed to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners or DIY users for a specific use case (e.g., home insulation, small-scale building).

arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect target segments (outdoor recreation and industrial workers).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum WTP (EUR) for each messaging condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Lifestyle messaging will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than compliance messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Compliance messaging will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than lifestyle messaging.

arguments.decision_rule: If lifestyle messaging achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and WTP ≥ €15, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If compliance messaging achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and WTP ≥ €15, pursue a compliance‑focused consumer line. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Ansell is focusing on core industrial and healthcare segments and exiting retail household gloves, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for a lifestyle proposition or willingness to pay a premium. A proposed test (Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Compliance Messaging) is needed to validate demand before committing.

Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public sources show Ansell is exiting retail household gloves and focusing on core industrial and healthcare segments, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand for a lifestyle proposition or willingness to pay a premium. A proposed test (Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Compliance Messaging) is needed to validate demand before committing.
arguments.target_customer: Individual consumers seeking lifestyle or functional protection for specific activities (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening).
arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer line positioned as a lifestyle or functional accessory, leveraging Ansell’s design and branding to capture premium pricing and repeat purchases.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week online survey test with 500 consumers, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay under lifestyle and compliance messaging.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a lifestyle proposition and willingness to pay a premium are unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows lifestyle messaging achieving purchase intent ≥ 40% and WTP ≥ €15, proceed to develop the differentiated consumer proposition.
If the test shows compliance messaging achieving purchase intent ≥ 40% and WTP ≥ €15, pursue a compliance‑focused consumer line.
If neither condition is met, abandon the differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on industrial and healthcare segments.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, leading to multiple purchases and premium pricing.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking style and protection; Ansell can capture value through premium pricing and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from utilitarian industrial/healthcare use to a lifestyle product changes purchase motivation from necessity to self-expression.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can sell higher-margin branded consumer lines and license its design to third-party brands, leveraging existing R&D capabilities.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for branded, stylish protective gloves.
The lifestyle positioning can be effectively communicated to individual buyers.
Ansell's design and manufacturing capabilities can be adapted for consumer products.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to purchase multiple pairs of branded protective gloves.
Sales of branded consumer gloves will show higher average transaction value compared to generic industrial gloves.
Competitor consumer protective brands will not capture the same market share as a differentiated Ansell offering.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, leading to multiple purchases and premium pricing.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a necessity for specific activities (e.g., cycling, gardening) where protection is critical, leading to repeat purchases for safety.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers engaged in activities requiring protection; Ansell can capture value through activity-specific positioning and repeat purchases.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from general industrial/healthcare use to activity-specific protection changes purchase motivation from general necessity to safety requirement.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can create bundled activity-specific lines and offer subscription or replacement services, leveraging existing R&D for functional performance.
assumptions: Consumers will purchase gloves specifically for activities where protection is essential.
Activity-specific messaging can effectively communicate safety benefits to individual buyers.
Ansell's functional capabilities can be adapted for activity-specific designs.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase gloves for specific activities where protection is critical.
Sales of activity-specific branded gloves will show higher repeat purchase rates compared to generic industrial gloves.
Competitor activity-specific brands will not capture the same market share as a differentiated Ansell offering.

arguments.objective: Determine whether Ansell Limited should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources for evidence; internal financial or contractual details may not be public.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current consumer reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, competitive advantage, or value capture.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, cycling, gardening) with unique features and branding.
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., general protective gear for non‑industrial consumers) using existing product lines.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial and healthcare segments, leveraging existing relationships and distribution.
4) Partner with or license the existing product portfolio to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a new consumer proposition.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, leading to multiple purchases and premium pricing.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking style and protection; Ansell can capture value through premium pricing and brand extension.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from utilitarian industrial/healthcare use to a lifestyle product changes purchase motivation from necessity to self-expression.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can sell higher-margin branded consumer lines and license its design to third-party brands, leveraging existing R&D capabilities.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for branded, stylish protective gloves.
The lifestyle positioning can be effectively communicated to individual buyers.
Ansell's design and manufacturing capabilities can be adapted for consumer products.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to purchase multiple pairs of branded protective gloves.
Sales of branded consumer gloves will show higher average transaction value compared to generic industrial gloves.
Competitor consumer protective brands will not capture the same market share as a differentiated Ansell offering.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated protective gloves if they perceive them as a necessity for specific activities (e.g., cycling, gardening) where protection is critical, leading to repeat purchases for safety.
arguments.who_benefits: Consumers engaged in activities requiring protection; Ansell can capture value through activity-specific positioning and repeat purchases.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Shifting from general industrial/healthcare use to activity-specific protection changes purchase motivation from general necessity to safety requirement.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Ansell can create bundled activity-specific lines and offer subscription or replacement services, leveraging existing R&D for functional performance.
assumptions: Consumers will purchase gloves specifically for activities where protection is essential.
Activity-specific messaging can effectively communicate safety benefits to individual buyers.
Ansell's functional capabilities can be adapted for activity-specific designs.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase gloves for specific activities where protection is critical.
Sales of activity-specific branded gloves will show higher repeat purchase rates compared to generic industrial gloves.
Competitor activity-specific brands will not capture the same market share as a differentiated Ansell offering.

X1.name: Precision vs. Health Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view a product description of a precision digital kitchen scale (high accuracy, fraction-of-a-gram resolution) and a health-focused version (carbohydrate counting, portion control). They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age (18–45). 150 per condition (precision and health messaging).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Precision messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than health messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Health messaging will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than precision messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for precision messaging is at least 10 points higher than for health messaging (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is <5 points, no expansion is recommended. If both conditions are met, prioritize the health‑focused proposition due to higher willingness to pay.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer proposition yet. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Mettler-Toledo International Inc. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for the manufacturer.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new features or services to existing customers (e.g., subscription models, data analytics).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current laboratory, industrial, and food retail B2B markets.
4) Change the sales route to individual buyers by partnering with retailers or using e‑commerce, without altering the product proposition.
5) Target a different customer group within the existing B2B base (e.g., small‑to‑medium food retailers) with a differentiated offering.

T1.claim: Home cooks and health-conscious consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale because they need precise weight measurement for recipes, portion control, and accurate nutrition tracking, and are willing to pay a premium for higher resolution and accuracy.
T1.who_benefits: Individual households, particularly those managing carbohydrate counting or following specific dietary guidelines.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Current kitchen scales often lack sufficient resolution (e.g., 0.1g vs. 0.5g) or are marketed as basic tools, making precise measurement difficult. A scale that measures to a tenth of a gram would eliminate uncertainty and improve accuracy.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can command premium pricing for a high‑resolution scale, sell through its direct channels, and capture repeat purchases for accessories or firmware updates.
assumptions: Consumers currently lack a suitable scale for precise measurement.
A premium price is acceptable for accuracy improvement.
Direct sales channel can reach individual buyers effectively.
predictions: In a test offering a 0.1g‑resolution scale at €150, at least 20% of surveyed households will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Purchase conversion will be higher among participants who cite recipe accuracy as a primary reason.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks and health-conscious consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale because they need precise weight measurement for recipes, portion control, and accurate nutrition tracking, and are willing to pay a premium for higher resolution and accuracy.

T2.claim: Small food retailers and restaurants will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale because it reduces labor costs, improves order accuracy, and enhances customer satisfaction, leading to higher sales volume and repeat purchases.
T2.who_benefits: Small food retailers, restaurants, and food service providers that handle multiple weight-based transactions daily.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Current manual weighing or low‑resolution scales cause errors, slow checkout, and increase labor costs. A scale that measures accurately and quickly would reduce errors and speed up transactions.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can sell through its direct channels or partner with retailers, offering volume discounts and recurring revenue from accessories or service contracts.
assumptions: Small retailers currently lack a suitable scale for weight measurement.
Labor cost reduction is a primary driver for adoption.
Retailers are willing to pay for a tool that improves operational efficiency.
predictions: In a pilot offering a 0.1g‑resolution scale to 50 small retailers, at least 30% will report a measurable reduction in checkout time or order accuracy within 12 weeks.
Retailers will be willing to pay a price premium of up to 20% over standard kitchen scales.

X1.name: Dual‑Channel Pilot: Consumer vs Retail Use Case
X1.method: Run a 12‑week pilot with two parallel test groups: (1) a consumer group receiving a 0.1g‑resolution digital kitchen scale via direct sales, and (2) a retail group receiving the same scale through a partner small‑food retailer. Both groups will be surveyed on purchase intent, willingness to pay, and primary purchase reason.
X1.sample: Consumer group: 200 households recruited via online panel (200 participants). Retail group: 50 small food retailers recruited via industry database, each receiving one scale and a 12‑week trial period.
X1.measure: Consumer group: purchase intent (binary: intent to buy) and stated willingness to pay (EUR). Retail group: average monthly order volume (units) and reported reduction in checkout time or order accuracy (self‑reported).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer group will show purchase intent ≥ 20% and willingness to pay ≥ €150, with recipe accuracy cited as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Retail group will show average monthly order volume ≥ 50 units and a self‑reported reduction in checkout time or order accuracy ≥ 15% among at least 30% of participants.

X1.decision_rule: If the consumer purchase intent threshold is met and willingness to pay is at least €150, proceed to develop a consumer proposition. If the retail threshold is met and at least 30% of retailers report measurable improvement, consider a retail‑focused pilot. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in either use case.

The proposed pilot (X1) is the next step to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before committing resources.

final.next_action: Run the 12‑week dual‑channel pilot (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay among consumers and retail partners, using the decision rule to decide on investment.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a premium 0.1g scale is uncertain; the pilot will resolve this. Retail adoption and willingness to pay are also uncertain.

If neither threshold is met, maintain focus on B2B markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Mettler-Toledo International Inc. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for the manufacturer.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new features or services to existing customers (e.g., subscription models, data analytics).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current laboratory, industrial, and food retail B2B markets.
4) Change the sales route to individual buyers by partnering with retailers or using e‑commerce, without altering the product proposition.
5) Target a different customer group within the existing B2B base (e.g., small‑to‑medium food retailers) with a differentiated offering.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers shift from using a general kitchen scale to a precision instrument for a specific task, they will be willing to pay a premium for accuracy and repeat the purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium price for the differentiated feature and sell through direct channels or retail partnerships, generating higher margins than standard scales.
assumptions: Consumers currently lack a reliable, precise kitchen scale for their specific use case.
A premium price is acceptable for the accuracy benefit.
Direct channels or trusted retailers can reach these consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a precision kitchen scale marketed for a specific use case, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a standard scale.
Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for the differentiated feature.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the product as a convenience item, sell through retail channels, and offer bundled solutions that include additional features like automatic tare or data logging, generating higher volume sales.

arguments.name: Precision vs. Convenience Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product offering and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel to represent general kitchen-scale users.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience variant will achieve higher purchase intent and WTP than precision variant.

arguments.decision_rule: If the precision variant's purchase intent exceeds the convenience variant's by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 20% higher, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case. If the opposite holds, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Mettler-Toledo International Inc. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home food weighing, personal fitness, or small‑business retail).

3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current laboratory, industrial, and food retail B2B markets.

5) Target a different customer group within the existing B2B base (e.g., small‑to‑medium food retailers) with a differentiated offering.
